text:
# Social robots used with older people: what has been studied, with whom, where, and what was found

**Scope and caveats.** I ran about 15 searches and read the full records, which here are abstracts, for about 22 papers. Many hits were attitude surveys, focus groups, design papers or ethics papers with no robot interaction, and I left those out. Items I only saw as search snippets are marked "lead". The database seems to under-represent recent work: I found almost no field studies of Pepper, and nothing on ElliQ. Most of the evidence is from 2004–2020.

## 1. Overview: the evidence base is mostly small and positive-leaning

- **Meta-analysis.** A review of 13 articles from 11 RCTs found positive trends for agitation, anxiety and quality of life, but none reached statistical significance in the pooled analysis [W2808281222].
- **Risk of bias.** Risk of bias was high, particularly for allocation concealment and blinding [W2808281222].
- **Narrative findings.** The narrative synthesis suggested improvements in engagement, interaction and stress indicators, and reductions in loneliness and medication use [W2808281222].
- **Conclusion.** The authors conclude the evidence is promising but limited by a lack of high-quality studies [W2808281222].
- **Other reviews to read.** These cover depression [W2889960145], dementia and ageing [W2888482633], scoping of socially assistive robots in elderly care [W2789445850], qualitative evidence on older adults' experiences [W2586081748], dog versus robot animal interventions [W2946010724], and barriers and enablers for humanoids [W2999297198].

## 2. Robots studied, by type

### A. Robot seal PARO (the best-evidenced robot)

**Participants and settings.** Participants are mostly people with dementia in nursing homes, day care and, less often, their own homes.

| Study | Design and setting | Main finding |
|---|---|---|
| Moyle et al. 2013 [W1488883230] | Pilot randomised crossover trial. 18 residents with mid-to-late dementia, one Australian aged-care facility. PARO compared with a reading group. | Moderate-to-large positive effect on quality of life and higher pleasure scores. The authors call for a larger trial. |
| Liang et al. 2017 [W2732925385] | Pilot block RCT, 30 dyads, 2 dementia day centres in Auckland plus participants' homes, 12 weeks. | Better facial affect and more communication with staff at the day centres. Participants with less cognitive impairment responded better. No significant differences in dementia symptoms or physiological measures. |
| Jøranson et al. 2020 [W3088196398] | Cluster RCT, 60 residents with dementia, 10 Norwegian nursing homes. PARO group activity twice a week for 12 weeks. | Actigraphy-measured sleep improved in the PARO group: higher sleep efficiency and total sleep time, fewer night awakenings. |
| Moyle et al. 2017 cluster-RCT [W2778691880] | Long-term care. PARO compared with a plush toy and usual care. | This record is a qualitative reflection on five participants, not the main outcomes. It reports large individual variation in response and ethical questions about giving PARO and taking it away. |
| Chen et al. 2020 [W3015603533] | Single-group before-and-after design with an observation phase. 20 older adults with depression, 4 Taiwanese long-term care facilities. Each kept PARO 24/7 for 8 weeks. | Depression and loneliness fell and quality of life rose during the intervention phase but not the observation phase. Interviews described PARO as humanised, a spur to social interaction, and a companion. |
| Valentí Soler et al. 2015 [W1807810766] | Quasi-experimental, about 100 nursing-home patients per phase plus day-care patients. 3 months. PARO, NAO and a real dog compared with control. | Apathy improved in the robot groups. Quality-of-life (QUALID) scores rose with PARO. The NAO group declined on one cognition measure (MMSE). Day-care results were mixed. |
| Wada & Shibata 2007 [W2043711811]; one-year follow-up [W2148142846] | Seal robots in a Japanese care house and a health service facility for the aged. | More social interaction and improved urinary stress-hormone reactions. |

**Other PARO leads (not read in full).**
- Naturalistic field studies in nursing homes [W2039822570, W2043587319].
- Group sensory therapy [W2040979576, W4243437205].
- Pain and mood qualitative work [W2985514812].
- Infection-control concerns [W3081435517].

**Interpretation for your project.** Effects are most reliable for affect, engagement and social behaviour. Effects on core dementia symptoms and physiological measures are inconsistent. Responses vary a lot between individuals, and people with milder impairment sometimes respond better.

### B. Other robot pets

- **AIBO.** A robotic dog and a live dog both reduced loneliness in long-term care residents compared with controls, and residents became attached to both. Attachment did not explain the loneliness reduction [W2132164645]. See also AIBO versus animal-assisted therapy in dementia [W1972564462] and an earlier robocat inquiry [W2074069593].
- **Joy for All animals (low-cost).** In a 6-month diary study in two supported-living sites, use grew over time and shifted from short sessions to near-permanent availability, so novelty-effect concerns were not borne out. Reported benefits were reminiscence, communication and possibly less agitation. Some users found the robots "creepy". The study is qualitative [W3015009700].
- **Robot cats at home.** A qualitative case study for people with dementia living at home [W3034490183].

### C. Humanoid and conversational companions

- **MARIO (Irish nursing home).** 10 residents with dementia had up to 12 sessions over 4 weeks. They showed sustained interest and more social engagement, but no significant change in quality of life, depression or perceived social support [W2955051104]. Related qualitative work is at [W3105249390, W2889731820].
- **Ryan Companionbot.** 6 residents with moderate dementia and/or depression in a Denver senior-living facility had 24/7 access in their rooms for 4–6 weeks. They built rapport and valued the robot. The evidence is observational and interview-based only [W2771925981].
- **NAO / Zora.**
  - Zora (a NAO with software) was monitored across 14 Dutch nursing-care organisations for two years. Staff reported barriers such as start-up time and software failures, and said the robot had a positive effect on clients and made work more fun for them [W2915888239].
  - NAO was also used in a theatre-based intervention in residential care. This is a conference abstract and a lead [W2982896790, W2899915867].
- **Brian 2.1 and Tangy (Toronto).**
  - Brian 2.1 was used for mealtime prompting with 8 residents aged 82–93. They were engaged, complied with the robot, and had positive attitudes towards it [W2112421347].
  - Tangy facilitates bingo [W2602852930, W1978404823]. A memory-game case study is at [W2003566851].
- **Exercise coach.** Fasola & Matarić's robot coach (two user studies with older adults) showed a strong preference for a relational over a non-relational coach, with high usability ratings [W2065178260]. See also [W1967507142].
- **Jibo-style robot in assisted living (lead).** An assisted-living study aimed at community-level connection between residents [W2943699887]. The abstract doesn't name the platform or give results, so I can't confirm either.
- **Chat robot in COVID-era care.** A "Sunshine" chat robot pilot for older adults with cognitive impairment [W3041860695]. This is a short letter and a lead.

### D. Home-deployed mobile service robots and telepresence

- **Hobbit (16 private households, over multiple weeks).** All users interacted with the robot daily, rated most functions as working well, and believed it would be part of future elder care. Adaptive behaviour eased interaction over time. Non-scripted interaction exposed real-world problems such as misinterpreted actions [W2994761079]. An earlier 18-household trial is at [W3137166629].
- **Giraff telepresence.** A year-long ecological case study with the MARTA assessment method [W2259814160]. Related: ROBIN [W2743226003] and a review of telepresence for dementia [W2751864896].
- **Social robot for patient-reported outcome measures.** 31 community-dwelling adults aged 70+ in a crossover study. Data reliability was 99.6% and usability averaged 80.1/100 [W2946005838].
- **Pepper.** The only Pepper-related hit is a protocol comparing a humanoid robot with tablet training for people with dementia at home [W2975531399]. I found no results papers.
- **Other leads.** Companion robot field tests in 8 homes [W2717439789]; in-home robots and sensors for older adults with depression [W2953482672]; a multicentre quasi-experimental study using the ICF framework [W2898061611]; engagement with SARs in home care [W2944083468]; a 3-month pilot of a robot to encourage social engagement in two long-term care sites [W3113108394]; and a long-term autonomous robot as a companion in physical therapy for dementia [W4251569456, W2592905630].

## 3. Cross-cutting patterns

1. **Settings.** Institutional settings (nursing homes, long-term care) dominate. Home trials are rarer and are usually usability or acceptance studies rather than outcome trials.
2. **Populations.** Dementia is the most-studied group, followed by depression and loneliness. Healthy community-dwelling older adults mostly appear in short usability studies.
3. **Outcomes.**
   - Positive and fairly consistent: engagement, affect and social interaction.
   - Plausible but based on few studies: sleep, loneliness, depression.
   - Weak or null: formal quality-of-life, dementia-symptom and physiological measures in several pilots [W2732925385, W2955051104].
4. **Method quality.** Most studies are pilots with small samples, short durations and no blinding. Many controls are usual care or a plush toy. Several of the strongest-sounding results come from uncontrolled before-and-after designs [W3015603533].
5. **Implementation.** Staff time, reliability, infection control and individual variation recur as practical issues [W2915888239, W3081435517, W2778691880].

## 4. Gaps to consider

- There are few RCTs of non-animal robots such as humanoids and conversational agents.
- Long-term (6 months or more) controlled data are scarce. The Joy for All diary study is the clearest long-term evidence and is qualitative.
- I found no home-based controlled trial with a humanoid.
- Recent platforms such as Pepper, ElliQ and Jibo are thinly covered here, so search them directly in other databases.

text:
# Social robots with people living with dementia: restricted evidence map

I re-screened everything from the first report and ran six new dementia-focused searches. I then read the full records (abstracts) for most of the studies below. I kept a study only if the participants were explicitly people with dementia, or a mixed group that includes them, and I flag the mixed groups. I left out attitude surveys, focus groups, design papers and studies of provider opinions.

## What I dropped from the first report

I removed these because their participants were not specifically people with dementia:
- Taiwanese PARO study in depressed older adults [W3015603533].
- Sung's PARO pilot in institutionalised older adults [W1510372641].
- Broadbent's multi-robot trial in a general aged-care facility [W1945345301]. It found no major benefits or problems.
- Zora in Dutch nursing homes [W2915888239].
- AIBO and loneliness [W2132164645].
- Brian 2.1 at mealtimes [W2112421347].
- Hobbit [W2994761079].
- Wada & Shibata's care-house studies [W2043711811].
- NAO theatre work [W2982896790].
- Thodberg's dog, robot seal and toy cat visits [W2294211165]. It is a randomised study of 100 nursing-home residents that recorded dementia diagnoses but was not restricted to dementia. It found that residents with greater cognitive impairment directed more interaction towards the animal and less towards people. It also found the robot seal failed to maintain attention over time. I can restore it if you want mixed nursing-home samples.
- Odetti's AIBO study [W2159536297]. Its title says "early dementia", but participants had MMSE above 23, so I treated it as mild cognitive deficits.

## 1. Controlled and randomised trials (all PARO)

| Study | Setting and sample | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Moyle 2013 [W1488883230] | Pilot randomised crossover trial. 18 residents with mid-to-late dementia, one Australian aged-care facility. PARO compared with a reading group. | PARO had a moderate-to-large positive effect on quality of life and higher pleasure scores. The authors say a larger trial is needed. |
| Liang 2017 [W2732925385]; thesis version [W2995685337] | Pilot RCT, 12 weeks. Dementia day-care centres and participants' homes in Auckland. The paper reports 30 dyads and the thesis reports 28. | Facial expressions and communication with staff improved at day care. People with milder impairment responded better. There were no significant differences in dementia symptoms or physiological measures. The thesis adds that caregiver burden and well-being also did not improve. |
| Jøranson 2020 [W3088196398]; thesis [W3102212853] | Cluster RCT. 60 residents, 10 Norwegian nursing-home special care units. PARO group sessions twice a week for 12 weeks. | Actigraphy showed better sleep: higher sleep efficiency and total sleep time, and fewer awakenings. The thesis also covers agitation, depression, psychotropic drugs and quality of life, but the abstract I retrieved doesn't give those results. |
| Pu 2020 [W3097289914], with qualitative arm [W2985514812] | Pilot RCT. 43 residents with dementia and chronic pain, 3 Australian nursing homes. Individual 30-minute sessions, 5 days a week for 6 weeks. | Observed pain was lower (PAINAD), and PRN (as-needed) medication use was lower. Staff-rated pain and regular medications did not differ. The 11 interviewed residents described mood and relaxation benefits and also complained about PARO's weight and voice. This is a conference abstract. |
| Moyle cluster-RCT [W2778691880] | PARO compared with a plush toy and usual care in long-term care. | The record I could retrieve is a qualitative reflection on five participants, not the main outcomes. It reports large variation in response, including different responses from the same person over time, and ethical issues around giving and withdrawing PARO. |

The first and third rows are the 2013 and 2020 trials. Several of these records describe the same trials as others (the Liang paper and thesis, the Jøranson paper and thesis, and the two Pu records), so don't count them as independent evidence.

## 2. Non-randomised comparisons and pilots

- **PARO, NAO and a real dog, Spain** [W1807810766].
  - Design: nursing-home units of about 100 patients per phase, plus day care, over 3 months, with blinded raters.
  - Findings: apathy improved in the robot groups. Quality-of-life (QUALID) scores rose with PARO. NAO was linked to a decline on one cognition measure (MMSE). Day-care results were mixed.
- **PARO in Korean nursing homes** [W2894885829].
  - Design: non-equivalent control group, 17 versus 16 residents, 12 sessions over 6 weeks.
  - Findings: positive emotions, social interaction and problem behaviours improved.
- **Companion robot in Hong Kong care homes** [W3111679151].
  - Design: participants with cognitive impairment, a childlike robot for 8 weeks, 28 completers of 48.
  - Findings: neuropsychiatric symptoms improved (NPI behaviour and distress). Daily living and depression did not. 43% were non-active users. The title says dementia but the sample is described as cognitive impairment. It is a conference abstract.
- **PARO versus a stuffed lion, Japan** [W1505024467].
  - Design: 30 residents, 19 with mild or moderate dementia and 11 with severe dementia, with video coding.
  - Findings: both groups talked more, laughed more and showed more positive emotion with PARO. Staff communication was higher with the lion in the mild-to-moderate group.
- **PARO, community-dwelling MCI or mild-to-moderate dementia** [W2080233792].
  - Design: single session, 11 participants (MMSE 9–24).
  - Findings: mostly feasible. Mood improved but not significantly. The sample is mixed MCI and dementia.
- **PARO versus a stuffed animal in occupational therapy** [W4407738599]. The authors concluded robot therapy encouraged more self-directed behaviour than the stuffed animal.
- **Robotic cat versus plush cat, special care unit** [W2074069593]. Both were linked to less agitation and more pleasure and interest, with similar trends for each.
- **AIBO, live dog and visitor alone** [W1972564462]. All visits stimulated interaction. AIBO and the live dog stimulated more than the visitor alone. AIBO produced longer looks and more resident-initiated conversation than the live dog.

## 3. Observational and field studies in care facilities

- **PARO sensory group therapy, US nursing home.**
  - Ten residents with varying levels of dementia over 7 weekly sessions. Social interaction rose and kept growing, so it wasn't just a novelty effect [W2040979576].
  - The 8-week companion report of the same programme found steadily more physical interaction and willingness to interact [W4243437205].
- **PARO in a nursing-home public area, 3 months** [W2039822570]. Interactions were rarely spontaneous, and staff or family mediation was central. The abstract doesn't say these residents had dementia, so this is a borderline inclusion.
- **Robot as walking-group assistant for advanced dementia** [W4251569456, W2592905630].
  - The robot accompanied weekly walking groups for a month. Therapists saw gains in motivation, group coherence and mood.
  - Technical unreliability turned the robot into extra workload for therapists.
  - Only 2 of 12 residents with advanced dementia started interactions themselves. Most interaction was prompted by therapists.
- **Matilda and similar baby-face robots in Australian residential care** [W2564685734, W2317990020].
  - Observational coding of engagement among 115 participants (2010–2013) in one paper, and 139 people with dementia over 5 years (robots named Sophie and Jack) in the other.
  - Both report improved emotional, visual and behavioural engagement and positive social engagement.
  - The samples probably overlap, but I couldn't confirm that.
  - These are observational studies with no control group.
- **Conversational robot in Alzheimer's disease** [W3033476063]. Pilot in a cognitive-assessment task. Conversations were better with human partners, but participants liked the robot and stayed interested despite miscommunication. Linguistic features may help monitoring.
- **AIBO in a nursing home** [W1178530349]. The robot was used as a shared focus of attention that started communication between residents who normally showed little interest in each other. The abstract is brief and gives no sample size.

## 4. MARIO (a European companion robot for dementia)

- **Irish nursing-home pilot** [W2955051104].
  - Design: 10 residents, up to 12 sessions over 4 weeks.
  - Findings: sustained interest and more social engagement, but no significant change in quality of life, depression or perceived social support.
- **Resilience multiple case study** [W3092218325].
  - Design: 10 people with dementia, 12 facilitated sessions.
  - Findings: resilience was supported in 8 of 10. People needed skilled facilitation to use MARIO.
- **Loneliness qualitative evaluation** [W2889731820] (conference abstract). Participants were mostly accepting, and the authors read this as supporting a role for companion robots against loneliness.
- **Multi-country qualitative study** [W3105249390].
  - Design: interviews in the UK, Italy and Ireland with 38 people with dementia and 69 relatives, carers and managers.
  - Findings: mostly positive. Voice recognition was a problem. Some staff worried that robots might replace care staff.

## 5. Home and community use

- **Robot cat at home** [W3034490183]. Qualitative case study of people with dementia and their families. Reported themes were distraction, communication, acceptance or rejection, and connecting with the cat and with others. Benefits were seen where the robot was accepted.
- **Betty in home-based care** [W2944083468]. Longitudinal study of engagement among people with dementia at home. The robot engaged them, and the authors argue for personalised content.
- **Matilda, 6-month home trial** [W1994379356]. Several Australian households. The authors report sensory enrichment, social connectivity and respite for partners. It is a systems paper, so the evidence is thin.
- **PARO at home** (within the Liang RCT above) [W2732925385].
- **Joy for All robot animals, 6-month diary study** [W3015009700]. Two supported-living sites for people with dementia or learning difficulties, so the sample is mixed. Use rose over time and shifted to near-permanent availability. Reported outcomes were reminiscence, better communication and possibly less agitation. A few people found the robots "creepy".
- **Ryan Companionbot** [W2771925981]. Six residents with moderate dementia and/or depression (a mixed sample) in a US senior-living facility, with the robot in their rooms 24/7 for 4–6 weeks. They built rapport with it and valued it. The evidence is observational and from interviews.
- **Protocol only** [W2975531399]. A humanoid robot versus tablet training for people with dementia at home (no results yet).

## 6. Patterns across the dementia studies

1. **PARO dominates.** Only PARO has several RCTs. NAO, MARIO, Matilda, Ryan, AIBO and the robot cats appear only in small, uncontrolled or qualitative studies.
2. **Consistent results.** Engagement, positive affect and social interaction (including with staff) recur across designs [W2732925385, W1505024467, W2894885829, W2040979576].
3. **Targeted outcomes.** The newer, more specific RCTs report effects on sleep [W3088196398] and on pain and PRN medication use [W3097289914]. Both are single trials with modest samples.
4. **Weak or null results.** Broad dementia-symptom, caregiver-burden and physiological measures often showed no difference [W2732925385, W2955051104, W2995685337].
5. **Who benefits.** Findings on severity point both ways:
   - Milder impairment predicted better response in Liang [W2732925385].
   - Both mild-to-moderate and severe groups showed more interest in PARO than in a toy in [W1505024467].
6. **Response varies a lot between individuals and over time** [W2778691880, W2985514812]. Some people also reject the robot [W3034490183, W3015009700].
7. **Facilitation matters.** Staff, therapists or family often drove interactions [W2039822570, W2592905630, W3092218325]. Autonomous or self-initiated use by people with advanced dementia was rare.
8. **Practical barriers.** These include reliability [W4251569456], voice recognition [W3105249390], PARO's weight and voice [W3097289914], and non-use (43% inactive users in [W3111679151]).
9. **Novelty.** Two studies suggest benefits persist: one over 7 to 8 sessions [W2040979576] and one over 6 months [W3015009700]. The seal-visit study found attention declined with PARO over time [W2294211165]. So the evidence on novelty is mixed.

## 7. Gaps and caveats

- I could not retrieve the main outcome paper of the Moyle cluster-RCT, which is the largest PARO trial against a plush-toy control. Search for it directly.
- Few studies include a control for the robot's interactivity, such as a plush toy. The exceptions are [W2778691880, W1505024467, W2074069593, W4407738599].
- There are no controlled trials of humanoid, conversational or telepresence robots in dementia.
- Home-based evidence is mostly qualitative or small.
- Several records are conference abstracts or theses [W3097289914, W3111679151, W2889731820, W3102212853]. I didn't see full-text methods or effect sizes for them.
- A related review is the telepresence-for-dementia integrative review [W2751864896]. It is a review rather than a study with participants, so I left it out.

I can focus on PARO trials only (including follow-up citations), build a table of outcome measures, or look for non-PARO platforms.

text:
I dropped more papers than my last message listed. That message named only some of them, and I removed the rest without saying so. Below is the full list from the first map. Most exclusions were judged on abstracts, and where I only saw a search snippet I say so.

## 1. Reviews and syntheses (dropped because they are not primary studies)
- [W2808281222] Meta-analysis of RCTs of social robots. I read the full record.
- [W2889960145] Depression review.
- [W2888482633] Review on ageing and dementia.
- [W2789445850] Scoping review of socially assistive robots in elderly care.
- [W2586081748] Qualitative evidence review.
- [W2946010724] Review of dogs and robot animals for residents with dementia in nursing homes.
- [W2999297198] Barriers and enablers for humanoid robots.
- [W2751864896] Telepresence for dementia, an integrative review.

I saw only snippets of all but the first. Two of these, [W2888482633] and [W2946010724], are dementia-specific, and the meta-analysis probably includes dementia RCTs (unverified). I think I was wrong to drop them. They are useful as pointers to primary studies.

## 2. Participants were not people with dementia (abstract read)

| Paper | Why dropped |
|---|---|
| [W3015603533] Taiwan PARO study | Participants were older adults with depression. |
| [W1510372641] Sung's PARO pilot | "Institutionalised older adults". The abstract doesn't mention dementia. |
| [W1945345301] Broadbent multi-robot trial | General aged-care residents and staff. |
| [W2915888239] Zora in Dutch nursing homes | The abstract doesn't specify client groups. |
| [W2132164645] AIBO versus live dog and loneliness | Long-term care residents, with no dementia criterion. |
| [W2112421347] Brian 2.1 at mealtimes | Eight residents aged 82–93, with no cognitive status given. |
| [W2294211165] Dog, PARO and toy cat visits | Mixed nursing-home residents, with dementia diagnoses recorded but not required. |
| [W2159536297] AIBO "early dementia" | Participants had MMSE above 23, so mild deficits at most. |
| [W2994761079] Hobbit field trial | Community-dwelling older adults in their own homes. |
| [W2946005838] Social robot collecting patient-reported outcomes | Community-dwelling adults aged 70+. |
| [W2717439789] Companion robot in homes | Eight self-supporting seniors living alone. |
| [W2953482672] PARO at home | Older adults with clinical depression. |
| [W2898061611] Japanese quasi-experimental study (ICF framework) | 67 nursing-home residents aged 65+ with three robot types. Dementia isn't mentioned. |
| [W3113108394] Robot engagement pilot in two long-term care sites | Ten of the participants had MCI and only one had Alzheimer's disease. |
| [W2943699887] Assisted-living social connectedness study | Not dementia-specific, and the abstract gives no robot name or results. |
| [W2259814160] Giraff long-term evaluation | Older adults at home. |

## 3. Dropped on a snippet or on the study type
- [W2043711811], [W2148142846] Wada & Shibata's care-house studies. Not dementia-specific. I read the first in full and saw only a snippet of the second.
- [W2982896790], [W2899915867] NAO theatre work. Conference abstracts, and dementia isn't mentioned.
- [W2602852930], [W1978404823] Tangy bingo and scheduling. Mostly system development.
- [W2003566851] Memory game case study in long-term care. Snippet only.
- [W2065178260], [W1967507142] Fasola & Matarić exercise coach. Older adults generally.
- [W3137166629] Earlier Hobbit trial. Snippet only.
- [W2743226003] ROBIN telepresence. Snippet only.
- [W3081435517] Disinfection of companion robots. Not a study with participants.

## 4. Cases where I was inconsistent or may have been wrong
- **[W2043587319]**, the PARO social-shaping study. I dropped it. Its sibling, the observational PARO study [W2039822570], is in the dementia map as a borderline inclusion. Neither abstract states that residents had dementia, so I should have treated both the same way. Both are borderline. Reinstate both or remove both.
- **[W3041860695]**, the "Sunshine" chat robot. It is a pilot with older adults with cognitive impairment in long-term care. The abstract is truncated, so I can't tell how many have dementia. I dropped it without flagging that. It is a lead worth checking.
- **[W3113108394]**. It has one participant with Alzheimer's disease and ten with MCI, so I judged it too far from dementia. It could reasonably be kept as an MCI-focused study.
- **Items I kept despite weak dementia criteria.** I kept some studies that don't strictly meet "people with dementia". They are listed in the dementia report with caveats:
  - [W3111679151], cognitive impairment.
  - [W2080233792], MCI plus dementia.
  - [W2771925981], dementia and/or depression.
  - [W3015009700], dementia or learning difficulties.
